title: India Won the 50-Over World Cup Last Year. In Four Days, They Start Chasing the T20 One.
excerpt: Harmanpreet Kaur leads India into the Women's T20 World Cup in England with a new-look squad, a 2-1 series loss to the hosts, and a question about her openers that everyone is asking.
body:
The ICC Women's T20 World Cup 2026 begins on June 12 in England, and India arrive as one of the tournament favourites — reigning 50-over world champions, a squad that has played together for years, and a captain in Harmanpreet Kaur who has been through this drill four times before.

But favourites is a complicated word in T20 cricket. India know this better than most.

Since the 2024 T20 World Cup, India have won 13 of 21 T20 internationals. That record is decent, not dominant. This year alone, they have managed only three wins in eight matches, including a 2-3 series loss to South Africa that exposed gaps in their middle-order finishing and death bowling. Then came a 1-2 bilateral series defeat to England — on the very pitches where the World Cup will be played.

For a team that dismantled South Africa in last year's ODI World Cup final, the T20 numbers are a reminder that the two formats inhabit different universes.

## The Opening Question

Former India captain Diana Edulji, one of the sharpest voices in Indian women's cricket, has zeroed in on the issue that will likely define India's campaign: the form of Smriti Mandhana and Shafali Verma at the top of the order.

"We need to just focus on our opening partnership," Edulji said. "Smriti and Shafali need to get quickly into form, and once they start getting into form, I think that will help India win."

https://www.instagram.com/p/DZSBKkxjV9y/

Mandhana and Verma have been central to India's white-ball identity for years. When they fire in the powerplay, the entire batting lineup breathes easier. When they do not, the pressure shifts downstream to Jemimah Rodrigues, Harmanpreet, and Richa Ghosh — players who are good enough to rescue innings but should not have to do it every game.

The England series underscored the concern. Neither opener made a significant impact across three matches, and India's totals suffered for it.

## The Squad

India's 15-member squad, announced by the BCCI in Mumbai, carries both continuity and a few calculated gambles. The headline selection is Nandni Sharma, a 24-year-old fast bowler from Chandigarh who earned her maiden call-up without a single international cap. In the WPL 2026, she took 17 wickets for Delhi Capitals in her debut season — the joint-highest in the tournament — and her pace and ability to swing the new ball impressed selectors enough to bypass more experienced options.

Yastika Bhatia and Radha Yadav return to the fold after missing recent series. Kashvee Gautam, who was widely expected to make the squad, missed out due to a right knee injury. Anushka Sharma and Uma Chetry were the notable omissions.

**Full squad:** Harmanpreet Kaur (c), Smriti Mandhana (vc), Shafali Verma, Jemimah Rodrigues, Deepti Sharma, Richa Ghosh (wk), Arundhati Reddy, Renuka Singh, Kranti Gaud, Shree Charani, Shreyanka Patil, Bharti Fulmali, Yastika Bhatia, Nandni Sharma, Radha Yadav.

## What Harmanpreet Knows

Harmanpreet's press conference at the ICC captains' event was revealing. She spoke less about tactics and more about the cultural momentum that her team has generated at home.

"We have seen that during last year's World Cup when we won. After that, we have seen massive change," she said. "Many girls, they are coming to play cricket, and I think when we do well a lot of things change, and hopefully, we play our best cricket and try to make impact on women's cricket."

This is not idle talk. The WPL's growth, the packed stands during the ODI World Cup, and the increasing visibility of women's cricket in India have given Harmanpreet's squad a platform that previous generations never had. A strong T20 World Cup campaign would solidify that — and a poor one would not undo it, but would certainly slow the momentum.

## The Group

India are in Group 1 alongside Australia, South Africa, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and the Netherlands. The fixture against Pakistan at Edgbaston on June 14 will dominate headlines, but the matches against Australia and South Africa will likely determine who advances and in what position.

Edulji is characteristically blunt about the Pakistan match: "I don't think, in women's cricket, Pakistan has any chance against us. Though there is hype for the match as usual, but I think we are far, far better." Her confidence reflects India's overwhelming record in the rivalry, but her broader point about T20 unpredictability is worth heeding: "The weakest team can also play well on that day and beat the strongest team."

## The Diaspora Angle

For NRIs in the UK, this is the most accessible major Indian cricket event in years. The tournament runs from June 12 to July 5, with matches across Birmingham, London, Nottingham, and other English cities. Unlike ICC events in the subcontinent or Australia, there are no midnight start times or clashing work schedules. For the estimated 1.8 million people of Indian origin in Britain, the matches are a short train ride away.

And there is more: after the T20 World Cup, India play a historic one-off Test against England at Lord's in July — the first women's Test ever staged at the ground. Edulji called it what it is: "It is the Mecca of cricket."

India are not short on talent, on occasion, or on platform. What they need now is a good first week.
